traveler: Isabelle Wilhelmine Marie Eberhardt (Si Mahmoud Saadi)
title: The Villa at the Grottes to the Wadi at Ain Sefra: Si Mahmoud Saadi and the Pages Taken Out of the Mud
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Geneva, rue de la Pepiniere: the birth in the villa Fendt
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a rented villa on the rue de la Pepiniere, in the working-class Grottes quarter under the railway, Nathalie de Moerder gives birth to a daughter and registers her as illegitimate: Isabelle Wilhelmine Marie Eberhardt, father unnamed. Nathalie has left the household of a Russian general, forty years her senior, for the family tutor, Alexandre Trophimowsky, an Armenian ordained Orthodox who became an atheist and an anarchist. He will raise the child and will never acknowledge her. The villa Fendt is demolished later; a street in the same quarter now carries her name.
suggested_refs: The site of the villa Fendt, rue de la Pepiniere, Les Grottes, Geneva, since demolished

stops.name: Villa Neuve near Geneva: the schoolroom of Alexandre Trophimowsky
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sources describe her home education as a condition of her whole childhood and give no dated schedule; this year stands for the middle of it
stops.campa: Outside the city, at the property the household calls Casa Bamba, Trophimowsky teaches the girl himself and lets no school near her. She reads Russian, French, German and Italian, construes Latin and Greek, and learns classical Arabic well enough to copy out the Qur'an in a clean hand. She digs the garden, saddles the horses, and wears her brothers' clothes because they are practical and because nobody in the house objects. Trophimowsky allows her no school and no church, and the household supplies her whole company.
suggested_refs: The Villa Neuve, called Casa Bamba, in the countryside outside Geneva

stops.name: Geneva, the half-sister struck off
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month given
stops.campa: Her half-sister Nathalie marries against Trophimowsky's wishes and is cut out of the household entirely, forbidden the door. The work of the house falls to the youngest daughter, who is eleven. The family contracts around its tutor: nine children scattered across three fathers, a mother going frail, a man who governs by doctrine and by silence. Isabelle keeps a notebook and writes letters to strangers outside the house. What she reads about is North Africa, which nobody in the household has seen.
suggested_refs: The Eberhardt-Moerder-Trophimowsky household accounts of the 1880s

stops.name: Geneva, the letters to an officer in the Sahara
stops.date_confidence: ceiling only: English Wikipedia dates the correspondence to 'sometime prior to 1894' and gives no start; this year is a placeholder beneath that ceiling
stops.campa: A French officer named Eugene Letord, garrisoned in the Sahara, places a newspaper advertisement asking for a pen pal. The girl in Geneva answers it. For years the desert reaches her as ink: heat, garrison boredom, the names of oases, the practical detail of how a European lives among Muslims and what it costs him. She has never seen a dune. She writes to him in a man's confidence and signs herself as she pleases. The correspondence will outlast the household it started in, and Letord will still be receiving her letters from Algerian ground.
stops.quote: Now more than ever do I realize that I will never be content with a sedentary life, that I will always be haunted by thoughts of a sun-drenched elsewhere.
stops.quote_source: Diary entry, The Nomad: The Diaries of Isabelle Eberhardt, trans. Nina de Voogd, ed. Rana Kabbani
suggested_refs: The Eberhardt-Letord correspondence, begun through a newspaper personal advertisement

stops.name: Geneva, Augustin runs for the Foreign Legion
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month given in sources consulted
stops.campa: Augustin, the brother she is closest to, is in debt and entangled with the Russian revolutionary emigres who pass through Geneva. He runs. The household learns afterward that he has enlisted in the French Foreign Legion and been shipped to Algeria. It is the moment North Africa stops being a subject and becomes an address, a real place where a person she loves eats and sleeps and is counted at roll call. She begins planning to follow him, and the plan does not take the shape of a visit.
suggested_refs: Augustin Eberhardt's Foreign Legion enlistment, c. 1894

stops.name: Sidi Bel Abbes, the Legion depot her brother is swallowed into
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Sidi Bel Abbes was the Legion's principal Algerian depot in this period, but Augustin's actual garrison is not attested in any source consulted, and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The Legion's Algerian home depot stands on the plateau south of Oran: barracks, a band, a parade ground, a wall of names, and the standing offer of a new identity to any man who wants one. Recruits shipped from Marseille are processed here before posting. Which garrison Augustin actually reached, no reachable source records. His sister will circle the Legion for the rest of her life: in Africa a European can be reissued as somebody else, and the paperwork agrees not to ask.
suggested_refs: The Quartier Vienot, Legion depot at Sidi Bel Abbes
sources: inference from Foreign Legion organization, cf. English Wikipedia, 'Isabelle Eberhardt'

stops.name: Geneva, the first byline: Nicolas Podolinsky
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month given
stops.campa: At eighteen she publishes her first short story in La Nouvelle Revue Moderne under the name Nicolas Podolinsky. The pseudonym is male and Russian, taken off the peg of her mother's country. This is not a disguise put on at the frontier of a strange land; it is her first byline, chosen before she has crossed any border at all. She signs nothing under her own name that year. She will go on choosing her signatures for the rest of her life, and the one she settles on, Si Mahmoud Saadi, is two years away.
suggested_refs: La Nouvelle Revue Moderne, 1895, first published story under the name Nicolas Podolinsky

stops.name: Geneva, Louis David photographs the sailor
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1895; no month given, and the month here is a placeholder
stops.campa: The photographer Louis David, who has lived in Bone, takes her portrait: cropped hair, a striped jersey and a sailor's collar, the flat stare of a young seaman off a Mediterranean packet. It is the image by which she will be known for a century. David and his family talk to her about Algeria and feed the appetite. The costume in this frame belongs to a studio. The traffic runs the other way soon enough: within two years she is dressed as a man in the street, in a country where the clothes carry a penalty.
suggested_refs: Louis David's 1895 studio portrait of Eberhardt in sailor's uniform

stops.name: Bone, the house on the rue Moreau
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1897; no precise day given
stops.campa: Mother and daughter land at Bone in May and lodge first with the Davids, then take an Arabic-style house on the rue Moreau, chosen deliberately outside the European quarter. Nathalie is failing. Isabelle is twenty. Within months she speaks Arabic well enough that strangers take her for a native speaker, and she is out in men's clothes on horseback in a colonial town that has opinions about both. Both women declare themselves Muslim. The French colony of Bone notes the household in its ledgers and does not forgive it.
suggested_refs: The Arab-quarter house on the rue Moreau, Bone (Annaba)

stops.name: Bone, the mother buried as Fatma Mannoubia
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1897; no precise day given, and the cemetery plot is not identified in sources consulted
stops.campa: In November Nathalie dies of a heart attack in the rue Moreau house. She is buried in Muslim ground as a convert, under the name Fatma Mannoubia. Trophimowsky arrives from Geneva after the burial and offers his daughter no comfort whatever; the two quarrel across the grave. Isabelle is twenty, in a foreign city, holding a conversion, a new name, an unfinished manuscript and no money. She writes that she wants to lie in the same kind of ground, and in seven years she will, six hundred miles west of here.
suggested_refs: The Muslim cemetery of Annaba and the grave of Fatma Mannoubia

stops.name: Bone, the taking of the name Si Mahmoud Saadi
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sources place the adoption of the name in the Bone years 1897-1899 without a precise date
stops.campa: She takes the name Si Mahmoud Saadi and wears it as she wears the burnous: not as a costume for expeditions but as her ordinary daily self, in the market, at the mosque, on horseback, in her correspondence. Men who know perfectly well who she is address her as Si Mahmoud and are not troubled by it. The French administration reads the clothes as an offence against public order and opens a file; the Sufi lodges read them as nothing very much. Asked by Europeans why she does it, she gives one answer and declines to elaborate on it.
stops.quote: It is impossible for me to do otherwise.
stops.quote_source: Her stock reply when asked why she dressed as an Arab man; quoted in Hedi Abdel-Jaouad, Isabelle Eberhardt (1993), p. 110
suggested_refs: The name Si Mahmoud Saadi, used in her correspondence, her travel and her burial inscription

segments.name: The Aures, and the Death of the Tutor

stops.name: Batna, the first year of wandering
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899; French Wikipedia gives no month
stops.campa: She moves inland to Batna, at the foot of the Aures, and begins the wandering that occupies the rest of her life: horseback, no fixed address, the hospitality of zawiyas and the floors of strangers. In the mountain towns she frequents Muslim mystical circles and asks to be taught. Money runs out and is not replaced. She smokes kief, drinks with soldiers, keeps poor company by every European standard on offer, writes every night, and is watched the whole time by people paid to write reports about her.
stops.quote: drank more than a Legionnaire, smoked more kief than a hashish addict and made love for the love of making love
stops.quote_source: A contemporary's description of her, quoted in Lesley Blanch, The Nine-Tenths Fabulous (2010), p. 266
suggested_refs: The Aures mountains and the mystical circles of Batna

stops.name: Geneva, Trophimowsky dying of throat cancer
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1899; no precise day given
stops.campa: Word comes that Trophimowsky is dying of throat cancer, and she returns to Geneva with Augustin to sit with the man who made her. He dies in May. He leaves an estate tangled in the claims of three families and nine children, and the litigation begins to eat it at once. The house that taught her six languages and dressed her as a boy closes for good. In the end she will inherit from him precisely what he meant her to have, which is the education, because the lawyers take everything else.
suggested_refs: The contested estate of Alexandre Trophimowsky, Geneva, 1899-1901

stops.name: Geneva, the engagement to Riza Bey
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899 only; the month is a placeholder and the sources give no date beyond the year
stops.campa: Between the funeral and the lawyers she is briefly engaged to Riza Bey, an Armenian diplomat, and then she is not. The record is thin: no letters, no reason given, a line in the chronology with nothing standing behind it. She is twenty-two and has buried both the adults who raised her inside two years. The estate is already in the hands of the lawyers, her brother is in France, and the household she grew up in has broken up for good. She goes to Paris to sell what she can write.
suggested_refs: The broken engagement to Riza Bey, Geneva, 1899

stops.name: Paris, the commission from the widow of the Marquis de Mores
stops.date_confidence: inferred: English Wikipedia gives no date for the Paris arrival or for the de Mores commission, only that she returned to Algeria in July 1900; this month is a placeholder for 'early 1900'
stops.campa: She arrives in Paris poor and stays poor, walking a city she detests to place articles nobody wants. Then the widow of the Marquis de Mores, a French aristocrat killed by his guides in the Sahara, hires her: go south, ask questions, find out who ordered it. It is the first time anyone pays her for the desert. She takes the commission and the money and converts both into a passage back to Algeria in July, which is what she wanted from the arrangement all along and made no secret of wanting.
stops.quote: The savage hatred I feel for crowds is getting worse, natural enemies that they are of imagination and of thought.
stops.quote_source: The Nomad: The Diaries of Isabelle Eberhardt, trans. Nina de Voogd, ed. Rana Kabbani
suggested_refs: The private inquiry into the 1896 murder of the Marquis de Mores in the Sahara

segments.name: The Souf, the Order, and the Sabre

stops.name: El Oued, the town sunk among dunes
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1900; no precise day given
stops.campa: She settles in July at El Oued in the Souf, a town of domed roofs half swallowed by sand, where the palms are planted in pits dug down to the water. She rents a house, keeps a horse, and lives on almost nothing at all. She has read about this country for ten years and written to a man garrisoned in it; now she draws its water and rides its roads. The de Mores inquiry gives her a licence to move among the tribes and question men, and the questioning is noticed by the French officers whose business it is to read other people's letters.
suggested_refs: The Souf oasis and the sunken palm gardens of El Oued

stops.name: El Oued, Slimene Ehnni of the spahis
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900; the month is a placeholder, as no source consulted dates the meeting more closely
stops.campa: Slimene Ehnni is a non-commissioned officer of the spahis, Algerian, French-schooled, of the Qadiriyya as she is, and the two begin living together openly. He is a colonial subject. She is a stateless European woman travelling as a Muslim man. The arrangement offends the administration on every axis it possesses, and the administration acts on the offence within a year. By the account of everyone who saw them it is a marriage in fact three years before it becomes one in law, and it holds until the night she dies.
suggested_refs: The spahi regiments of the Souf and the household of Slimene Ehnni

stops.name: El Oued, initiation into the Qadiriyya
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900; Wikipedia gives no more precise date and the month here is a placeholder
stops.campa: Sheikh Hussein ben Brahim initiates her into the Qadiriyya, waiving the examination the order usually requires, and she is received as Si Mahmoud. The tariqa is the oldest in Islam and the deepest rooted in Algeria: the order whose Algerian shaykh-line produced Emir Abdelkader, whose father headed its zawiya on the Wadi al-Hammam and who carried its discipline through seventeen years of war against the French army. She takes its litanies and its obligations. The officers reading her mail refile her as a religious problem as well as a political one.
suggested_refs: The Qadiriyya lodges of the Souf and the chain of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani

stops.name: Touggourt, a waypoint on the Souf road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a plausible waypoint on her attested Souf itinerary, not confirmed by name or date in any source consulted; the date is a placeholder
stops.campa: The oasis on the road north out of the Souf: salt, dates, garrison, caravans coming up from the palm country. Her itinerary in these years runs through towns exactly like this one, days in the saddle between wells, nights in a zawiya or a cafe or the open, the horse watered before the rider. No source consulted places her in Touggourt on a dated day. It stands here for the travelling itself, which is most of what she did in these two years and almost none of what anybody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The caravan roads of the Souf between Touggourt and El Oued
sources: general geography of her attested Souf travels; no direct citation located

stops.name: Behima, the sabre at the Qadiriyya gathering
stops.date_confidence: attested: French Wikipedia gives 29 January 1901; English Wikipedia has only 'late January 1901'. The identification of Behima with the modern commune of Hassani Abdelkrim rests on the Eberhardt articles alone
stops.campa: At a Qadiriyya gathering at Behima she is asking the marabout Si Lachmi for money when a man named Abdallah ben Mohammed comes at her with a sabre. The first blow glances off her head; the second opens her left arm to the bone. Bystanders take him. She is twenty-three, and she lives. Biographers have blamed a rival Sufi order hostile to her closeness with the Qadiriyya, and others have blamed the French administration, which wanted her out of the country; the sources do not settle it. The attacker offers one explanation and repeats it.
stops.quote: God wished it; God still wishes it.
stops.quote_source: Abdallah ben Mohammed's repeated answer when asked why he attacked her; quoted in Cecily Mackworth, The Destiny of Isabelle Eberhardt (1977), p. 111
suggested_refs: The village of Behima, present-day Hassani Abdelkrim, east of El Oued

stops.name: El Oued, the military hospital and the miracle
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1901; no precise day given
stops.campa: She is carried to the military hospital at El Oued and mends slowly; the arm never fully recovers its strength. The Qadiriyya of the Souf read her survival as a mark of favour and raise money to keep her, which is how she eats through the winter. The French authorities read the identical event as a scandal and a thickening file. Both readings are about her, and neither of them consults her. From the bed she writes, and asks after Ehnni, who has been posted away from her by an army that has understood the situation perfectly.
suggested_refs: The military hospital at El Oued, February 1901

stops.name: Marseille, the docks in her brother's clothes
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1901; no precise day given
stops.campa: Ordered out of North Africa without explanation and without charge, she crosses to Marseille and moves in with Augustin and his wife. She works the docks beside her brother as a labourer, in men's clothes and under a man's name, unloading ships that come from the country she is forbidden to enter. The Legion took her brother and gave him Algeria; the administration has taken Algeria from her and given her the Vieux-Port. She writes appeals that go unanswered and waits for the trial that will readmit her for a week.
suggested_refs: The Vieux-Port of Marseille and the dock labour of the Eberhardt siblings, 1901

stops.name: Constantine, forgiving the man who tried to kill her
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1901; no precise day given, and Encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia differ on the original sentence
stops.campa: Summoned back from France to testify against Abdallah ben Mohammed at Constantine, she tells the court she bears him no grudge and asks for mercy on his behalf. The sentence, given as penal servitude for life, is later commuted to ten years. Her testimony impresses nobody in the administration, which escorts her out of the country again the moment she has stopped being useful to it. Inside six months she has been attacked, expelled, recalled to give evidence and expelled again, and she holds no nationality that any of these officials is obliged to respect.
suggested_refs: The 1901 assize trial of Abdallah ben Mohammed at Constantine

stops.name: Marseille, the marriage that makes her French
stops.date_confidence: attested: French Wikipedia gives 17 October 1901; English Wikipedia gives only 'October 1901'
stops.campa: Slimene Ehnni is transferred to a spahi regiment near Marseille, and on the seventeenth of October they marry. He holds French status; the marriage confers it on her, which no amount of argument had done, and no French administrator may now expel a Frenchwoman from French Algeria. The colonial order left one door open in its own rules, and she walks through it with the paperwork in order. Her way home has become a matter of one certificate, signed and stamped in the correct office.
stops.quote: For those who know the value of and exquisite taste of solitary freedom (for one is only free when alone), the act of leaving is the bravest and most beautiful of all.
stops.quote_source: The Nomad: The Diaries of Isabelle Eberhardt, trans. Nina de Voogd, ed. Rana Kabbani
suggested_refs: The Marseille marriage register, 17 October 1901

stops.name: Geneva, the estate sold and nothing left
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1901; no month given in sources consulted, and this month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The Geneva property is sold at last, and the proceeds of Trophimowsky's estate go entirely to the lawyers who have spent two years quarrelling over it. Nothing at all reaches her. She had counted on this money, and the counting had shaped several years of plans, including where she would live and what she would write. From here she lives on journalism, on her husband's small pay, and on the hospitality of religious houses, which is to say on other people, deliberately and without apologising for it.
suggested_refs: The final liquidation of the Trophimowsky estate, Geneva, 1901

stops.name: Bone, home to her husband's family
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1902; no precise day given
stops.campa: Ehnni is discharged from the army and the couple return to Bone, to his family's house, in the city where her mother lies under a Muslim name. She is twenty-five and has been out of Algeria for nine months, the longest exile of her adult life. The family takes her in as Si Mahmoud's other self, wife and stranger in the same room. She has a husband, a nationality, an arm that aches in the cold and no money whatever, and she starts hunting for newspaper work the week she lands.
suggested_refs: The Ehnni family house at Bone (Annaba)

stops.name: Algiers, Victor Barrucand and Al-Akhbar
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1902; no precise day given
stops.campa: Victor Barrucand takes her onto the newspaper Al-Akhbar, and for the first time in her life she is paid to write. Barrucand is a French anarchist, a publisher, a man with theories about Algeria and firm views about literary property. He prints her, edits her, and will one day set his own name beside hers on books she is not alive to correct. She travels for him and files copy from wherever she has got to. The desert has acquired an office, and the office pays for the horse and the paper.
suggested_refs: The offices of Al-Akhbar, Algiers, under Victor Barrucand

stops.name: Tenes, the translator's post and the fevers
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1902; no precise day given
stops.campa: Ehnni is hired as a translator at Tenes on the coast and she follows him into a small colonial town of officials, feuds and denunciations, where a European woman in a burnous is the principal event of the season. She writes, quarrels with the local administration, and leaves as often as she can arrange to. Malaria has settled into her and returns in cycles; the fevers, the kief, the tobacco and the chosen poverty are all working on a body that is twenty-five years old and already behaving like an older one.
suggested_refs: The colonial administration of Tenes, 1902-1903, and its quarrels with the Ehnni household

stops.name: El Hamel, the zawiya of Lalla Zaynab
stops.date_confidence: range only: the source dates the visits to the broad period when she was based in Algiers, c. 1900-1903, and gives no year or month
stops.campa: Ten kilometres south-west of Bou Saada stands the Rahmaniyya zawiya of El Hamel, and at its head sits Lalla Zaynab, who refused to marry, took her dead father's place against her cousin's claim, and governs the lodge in her own name. Eberhardt rides out to see her more than once and writes her down carefully: a woman of great simplicity, with a sadness visible behind the intelligence. She comes away rejuvenated, she says. Zaynab holds the lodge until her death in 1904. Eberhardt rides back to Algiers.
suggested_refs: The Rahmaniyya zawiya of El Hamel and the shaykha Lalla Zaynab

stops.name: Algiers, Trimardeur begins to appear
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1903; no precise day given
stops.campa: Her novel Trimardeur starts running in serial: the story of a Russian student who throws over Europe for hard labour and the open road, written by a woman who has done the same thing and is still doing it. She is filing journalism at the same time, keeping the diaries she calls her journaliers, and drafting the sketches of Algerian life that will be published after her death under arrangements she never agreed to. The output is large, the fee is small, and the manuscripts ride with her in a saddlebag.
stops.quote: I will only ever be drawn to people who suffer from that special and fertile anguish called self-doubt, or the thirst for the ideal, and desire for the soul's mystical fire. Self-satisfaction because of some material accomplishment will never be for me. The truly great are those who quest for better spiritual selves.
stops.quote_source: The Nomad: The Diaries of Isabelle Eberhardt, trans. Nina de Voogd, ed. Rana Kabbani
suggested_refs: Trimardeur, serialised from August 1903

stops.name: The Zousfana valley near Taghit, after El-Moungar
stops.date_confidence: inferred: English Wikipedia says only that Barrucand dispatched her to report on the aftereffects of the 2 September 1903 battle, with no date of arrival. The coordinates are a reconstruction placed in the Zousfana valley near Taghit; no reliable coordinate for the El-Moungar site was locatable, and the English Wikipedia infobox coordinate for the battle is demonstrably wrong by hundreds of kilometres
stops.campa: Barrucand sends her south-west to the Moroccan frontier to report on the aftermath of El-Moungar, where on the second of September a convoy escort was cut to pieces in the Zousfana valley, thirty-six dead and most of the officers among them. She arrives after the burials, into a country of blame and reinforcement. The disaster costs the commander of the Ain Sefra region his post. The officer sent to replace him is Hubert Lyautey. Her war reporting and his command begin in the same wreckage, a few weeks apart.
suggested_refs: The El-Moungar engagement of 2 September 1903 and the replacement of the Ain Sefra command

stops.name: Beni Ounif, the general and the informant
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1903 by French Wikipedia at Beni Ounif; Encyclopedia.com dates their first meeting to 'late 1903', arranged through Barrucand, and no precise day is given
stops.campa: At Beni Ounif, on the frontier road between Ain Sefra and Bechar, she meets General Lyautey. He is newly in command of a region in revolt and needs someone who can go where his officers cannot and return with the truth about a marabout's intentions. She is twenty-six, penniless, ill, and can do exactly that. He pays her and sends her out on missions, and after her death he writes to Barrucand about her as a friend. She takes the money and rides where he points her.
stops.quote: We understood each other very well, poor Mahmoud and I, and I shall always cherish exquisite memories of our evening chats. She was what attracts me most in the world: a rebel.
stops.quote_source: General Hubert Lyautey, letter to Victor Barrucand after her death, quoted in Jamie James, The Glamour of Strangeness (2016)
suggested_refs: Lyautey's Ain Sefra command and his correspondence concerning Eberhardt
sources: Jamie James, The Glamour of Strangeness (2016)

stops.name: Kenadsa, weeks inside the Ziania zawiya
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the visit is a well-known episode resting on her own published Saharan writing; the Wikipedia article on Kenadsa does not mention her, and no independently dated source was reachable, so the date is a placeholder
stops.campa: She rides into the Ziania zawiya at Kenadsa, a ksar village of black stone near the Moroccan border, and stays for weeks among the students and the sick, in the courtyards, sleeping badly and taking notes. It is the last sustained writing she does: a long account of a desert lodge, its silences, its hierarchies, its heat, its beggars. She is the guest of an order and the informant of a French general in the same season, and leaves no sign of finding that a contradiction worth arguing out on paper.
suggested_refs: The Ziania zawiya at Kenadsa and Eberhardt's account of her stay

stops.name: The Ksour range, the errand for Lyautey
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the site of this mission is not named in any source consulted; the coordinates are a rough placeholder for the Saharan Atlas and Ksour range, and the month is inferred from her arrival at the Ain Sefra hospital in October
stops.campa: Lyautey sends her into the mountains to talk with an influential marabout on his behalf, the kind of errand no officer of his could perform and no ordinary traveller would survive. She goes. The fever goes with her. Which massif, which lodge and which man are recorded nowhere reachable; the mission survives in the record only through its result, which is that she comes back weakened and does not get better afterward. The Ksour range stands here for a journey that nobody thought to write down at the time.
suggested_refs: The marabout missions undertaken for the Ain Sefra command, 1904

segments.name: Ain Sefra: the Wadi Comes Down

stops.name: Ain Sefra, discharging herself from the hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1904; no precise day given in sources consulted, and this day is a placeholder
stops.campa: She is admitted to the military hospital at Ain Sefra in October: thin, malarial, probably syphilitic, twenty-seven years old. The doctors want to keep her in. She discharges herself against their advice, because Slimene has been posted to the town and she means to live with her husband rather than in a ward. It is the last decision she makes for herself. She has not once in her adult life stayed where she was told to stay, by a doctor or by an administration.
suggested_refs: The military hospital at Ain Sefra, October 1904

stops.name: Ain Sefra, the mud house in the lower town
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twentieth she and Ehnni rent a small mud-brick house in the lower town, down where the ground flattens toward the bed of the wadi. They own almost nothing: her papers, his pay, a few pots. She is too weak now to ride. The town lies between the Ksour range and the dunes, in a country where rain is an event people date their lives from, and the watercourse that gives Ain Sefra its name is a stony channel of nothing at all for most of any given year.
suggested_refs: The lower town of Ain Sefra and the bed of the Oued Sefra

stops.name: Ain Sefra lower town, the flash flood
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rain falls in the mountains and comes down the wadi in the night as a wall of water. The flood takes the lower town: the mud walls dissolve, the roofs fall in, and the house Isabelle Eberhardt has lived in for one day collapses on top of her. Slimene gets out. She is found under one of the supporting beams. She is twenty-seven years old. Whether she tried to run or lay still is disputed by every biographer who has written about her, and the only witness who was in the room could not say.
stops.quote: Soon, the solitary, woeful figure that I am will vanish from this earth, where I have always been a spectator, an outsider among men.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Eberhardt; full text as given in Emma Garman, 'Feminize Your Canon: Isabelle Eberhardt', The Paris Review, 11 February 2019
suggested_refs: The Ain Sefra flood of 21 October 1904

stops.name: Ain Sefra, the body brought out on the sixth day
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia; English Wikipedia does not give the recovery date
stops.campa: The water drains away and leaves a town of collapsed mud and standing silt. The digging goes on for days. Her body is not brought out of the wreckage until the twenty-seventh, six days after the flood. Soldiers of the Ain Sefra garrison do the work, under orders from the general who had been sending her into the mountains two months earlier. Of the whole small household there is nothing to recover but a body and a quantity of wet paper trodden into the mud of the lower town.
suggested_refs: The recovery operations at Ain Sefra, 21-27 October 1904

stops.name: Ain Sefra, the pages gathered out of the silt
stops.date_confidence: attested to late October 1904; no precise day given in sources consulted
stops.campa: Lyautey orders his troops to search the silt for her manuscripts, and they do it: sheet by sheet out of the mud of a wrecked town, the diaries and the drafts and the unfinished Trimardeur, torn, illegible in places, incomplete. What comes out is dried, gathered and posted to Victor Barrucand in France. No source gives a count of the pages saved or of the pages lost. Everything published under her name from this day forward passes first through the hands of the man who opened that parcel.
suggested_refs: The manuscript recovery ordered by Lyautey and the parcel sent to Victor Barrucand

stops.name: Sidi Boudjemaa, the stone with two names
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1904; the day is a placeholder and the cemetery coordinates are approximate, taken as a westward offset from the Ain Sefra town centre
stops.campa: She is buried in the small Muslim cemetery of Sidi Boudjemaa, west of the town, under the name she chose for herself. Lyautey has a marble stone cut and set over her: Si Mahmoud Saadi in Arabic, Isabelle Eberhardt in French, the two names on one slab with neither cancelling the other. She had wanted Muslim ground and she has it, six hundred miles west of the grave in Bone where her mother lies as Fatma Mannoubia. She was twenty-seven, and she had been in Algeria for seven years.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Si Mahmoud Saadi in the cemetery of Sidi Boudjemaa, Ain Sefra

stops.name: Algiers, the books assembled by Victor Barrucand
stops.date_confidence: attested: the BnF catalogue lists the first Fasquelle edition of Dans l'ombre chaude de l'Islam in 1906, with reissues in 1908, 1911, 1921 and 1923. French Wikipedia's 1921 is a reissue and Encyclopedia.com's November 1905 is not borne out by the catalogue
stops.campa: Barrucand reconstructs the mud-damaged papers into a book, Dans l'ombre chaude de l'Islam, published in 1906 to acclaim and steady sales. More volumes follow: Notes de route in 1908, Mes Journaliers in 1923, Au Pays des sables in 1925, Pages d'Islam in 1932. He prints his own name beside hers as co-author and does not mark where her sentences stop and his begin. The manuscripts he worked from were torn and silted, and no one since has been able to separate the two hands.
suggested_refs: Dans l'ombre chaude de l'Islam, Eberhardt and Barrucand, E. Fasquelle, 1906

stops.name: Tangier, Paul Bowles reads her and starts translating
stops.date_confidence: attested for the biography: Open Library records Cecily Mackworth's The Destiny of Isabelle Eberhardt as first published in 1951 by Routledge and Kegan Paul, and the English Wikipedia article's 1954 is an error. The Bowles translations followed over subsequent years and are not dated to 1951
stops.campa: Cecily Mackworth publishes The Destiny of Isabelle Eberhardt and the dead woman comes back into circulation. Paul Bowles, living in Tangier, reads her and begins putting her into English: the desert sketches, the diaries, the pieces Barrucand had rearranged. Half a century after the flood she is being read in a language she never wrote a line of, by people looking for what she went looking for. Biographies, a play, a film, a graphic series and an opera follow across the next seventy years.
suggested_refs: Cecily Mackworth, The Destiny of Isabelle Eberhardt (1951); Paul Bowles's English translations from Tangier
sources: Open Library record, Mackworth, The Destiny of Isabelle Eberhardt

stops.name: Algiers, the street that peters out
stops.date_confidence: undated: no source consulted gives a year for any of these namings beyond 'twentieth century'; this date is a placeholder marker only
stops.campa: A street in Algiers is named for Isabelle Eberhardt, another in Bechar, and a third in the Grottes quarter of Geneva a few hundred metres from the demolished villa where she was born. A memorial garden is set aside on the Avenue Foch in Paris, between numbers 46 and 50. Of the Algiers street, one contemporary recorded what it does at the far end. Three countries, four namings and a marble slab in a desert cemetery, for a woman who spent her whole adult life refusing a fixed address.
stops.quote: begins in an inhabited quarter and peters out into a wasteland
stops.quote_source: A contemporary writer's description of the street named for Eberhardt in Algiers, quoted in Lesley Blanch, The Nine-Tenths Fabulous (2010), p. 271
suggested_refs: Rue Isabelle-Eberhardt, Les Grottes, Geneva; the Eberhardt streets of Algiers and Bechar; the Avenue Foch memorial garden, Paris
